newsitem.title: USA: USDA estimates neutral for cotton market-analysts.
newsitem.headline: USDA estimates neutral for cotton market-analysts.

text.p: Cotton analysts expect U.S. Agriculture Department's estimates for the new crop to have a marginal influence over the market, as the slightly bearish U.S. numbers could be canceled out by the positive world numbers.
"It's a wash," said Sharon Johnson, an analyst with Frank Schneider and Co Inc. "The USDA raised U.S. stocks next year, but lowered world stocks."
U.S. ending stocks are expected to reach 4.25 million bales, compared with 4.05 million bales this season. World stocks are expected to fall one million bales to 36.54 million bales in 1997/98.
The reduction in the world number came in part from an increase in world consumption to a projected 88.5 million bales in 1997/98 from 86.44 million bales in 1996/97.
"The USDA must see a healthier economy and lower prices fostering greater demand," Smith Barney analyst David Brandon said.
He expects the report will have a "marginal" effect on prices, which are more apt to be driven by weather and prices at this point.
USDA pegged U.S. output in 1997/98 at 18.5 million 480-lb bales, compared with estimates that ranged from 17.96-18.8 million bales.
Exports were seen at 7.3 million bales compared with estimates of 6.0-7.2 million bales.
Analysts stressed that these initial numbers are apt to change dramatically during the season, as weather and pest-related problems arise.
Also, USDA's estimate for planted area of 14.485 million acres, on which today's numbers are based, is expected to decline in the next report.
Since USDA issued the estimate in March, heavy rain has delayed planting in Texas and the Southeast, and high soybean prices and weak cotton futures have made cotton less attractive to farmers.
